title: Balancing FSc Boards and MDCAT Prep at the Same Time
excerpt: The traditional gap between FSc boards and MDCAT is shrinking — which makes parallel preparation less of an optional strategy and more of a necessity. Here's how to actually do both at once.

content.text: Why this question matters more than it used to

For years, the standard MDCAT playbook was sequential: finish your FSc boards, then spend several dedicated months preparing for MDCAT afterward. That gap is currently in flux — PMDC has announced changes intended to significantly shorten the traditional period between FSc results and the MDCAT exam, with the stated goal of reducing reliance on expensive post-boards coaching. Exactly how much the gap shrinks, and for which exact session, has been reported inconsistently across different sources and has been a source of real confusion and anxiety among students.

Don't plan your year around a specific "days after boards" or "months after boards" figure you've seen in a news article or blog post, including this one. Confirm the current, officially notified MDCAT date relative to your own FSc board schedule directly from PMDC before building your calendar around it — and build in the assumption that the gap may be shorter than it has been in past years.

Whatever the exact final gap turns out to be for your session, the direction is clear enough to act on: you can no longer safely assume you'll get months of dedicated post-boards time to prepare for MDCAT. Parallel preparation — studying for both at once — has gone from "a smart strategy for ambitious students" to something much closer to a necessity.
The good news: the overlap is larger than it looks

Here's what makes parallel prep genuinely workable rather than just exhausting: FSc and MDCAT aren't really two separate bodies of content competing for your time. MDCAT is drawn directly from your FSc Biology, Chemistry, and Physics syllabus — the same chapters, the same core concepts. Studying a chapter well enough for your board exam and studying it well enough for MDCAT overlap far more than they conflict.

The real difference isn't what you study — it's how you're tested on it. Board exams often reward reproducing material the way it was taught: writing out a derivation, explaining a process in your own words, answering long-form questions. MDCAT tests the same underlying content through multiple-choice questions that often apply a concept in an unfamiliar way or connect ideas across chapters. That distinction is the key to studying efficiently for both at once.
A practical way to combine both
Rather than treating FSc revision and MDCAT prep as two separate to-do lists, build a single study pass for each chapter that covers both formats:

items: Learn and understand the chapter thoroughly first — this serves both exams equally, since neither can be faked with surface-level familiarity
Once you're confident in a chapter, do a board-style review pass (long-form questions, past board papers, definitions and derivations you might need to write out)
Then do an MDCAT-style review pass on the same chapter (timed MCQs, application-based questions, past MDCAT papers on that topic)

content.text: This means each chapter effectively gets covered once for understanding, then twice more for the two different question formats — which takes real time, but far less than studying the same content twice from scratch as if they were unrelated subjects.
Don't let MDCAT MCQ practice crowd out board-specific skills

One risk of parallel prep, especially once MDCAT starts feeling more urgent, is unconsciously drifting all your practice time toward MCQs and neglecting skills your board exam specifically requires — writing full derivations, structuring long-form answers, or explaining a process clearly in your own words. These are skills that fade without practice just like anything else, and a strong MDCAT-style understanding of a topic doesn't automatically transfer into a well-structured board exam answer.

Keep a portion of your study time, even if it's a smaller portion as boards approach, dedicated specifically to board-exam-style practice — past board papers, timed long-answer practice, and reviewing how marks are actually awarded on board exam answers.
A few practical habits make the juggling more manageable:

items: Keep a single combined calendar, not two separate ones for "FSc study" and "MDCAT study" — trying to mentally track two parallel schedules is its own source of unnecessary stress
As board exams get closer, it's reasonable to temporarily shift more weight toward board-specific practice — this isn't abandoning MDCAT prep, since the underlying content study still carries over

Immediately after boards finish, don't take an extended break assuming you'll have months to recover before MDCAT prep needs to ramp back up — with a shorter post-boards gap, that recovery time may not be available the way it used to be

If you can, start light MDCAT-style MCQ practice on chapters well before your boards are even finished, even if it's just a small amount alongside board revision — this reduces how much you'll need to compress into whatever gap remains afterward

content.text: Studying for two overlapping-but-different exams at once, especially under real time pressure, carries a real risk of burnout if it's not managed deliberately. Build in actual rest, not just shorter study sessions — a fully depleted student close to boards performs worse on both the board exam and any MDCAT prep happening alongside it. Sustainable pacing over many months tends to beat an unsustainable pace that collapses right when you need to perform.

The traditional model of "finish boards, then prepare for MDCAT" is no longer a safe assumption to build your year around. The overlap between FSc and MDCAT content is large enough that parallel preparation isn't as inefficient as it might sound — a single thorough study pass per chapter, followed by separate board-style and MDCAT-style practice on that same material, covers both exams without duplicating your effort from scratch. Keep a close eye on the actual, officially confirmed schedule for your specific session rather than assuming a gap you've read about elsewhere applies to you, and build in real rest so you're not running on empty right when both exams matter most.

items.question: Is the gap between FSc boards and MDCAT really shrinking?
items.answer: PMDC has announced changes intended to significantly shorten this gap, aimed at reducing reliance on post-boards coaching academies. The exact timeline has been reported inconsistently across sources — confirm the current officially notified date directly from PMDC rather than relying on any single report, including this one.

items.question: Do I need to study FSc and MDCAT content separately?
items.answer: Not entirely. MDCAT draws directly from the same FSc Biology, Chemistry, and Physics syllabus, so the underlying content overlaps heavily. What differs is how each exam tests it — board exams reward reproducing material as taught, MDCAT tests it through application-based MCQs.

items.question: How should I structure study time to cover both exams efficiently?
items.answer: Do one thorough pass to understand each chapter, then a board-style review pass (long-form questions, past board papers) and a separate MDCAT-style review pass (timed MCQs, application questions) on the same material — rather than studying each exam's content from scratch separately.

items.question: Should I start MDCAT MCQ practice before my FSc boards are finished?
items.answer: It can help. Starting light MDCAT-style practice on chapters already covered, even in small amounts alongside board revision, reduces how much needs to be compressed into whatever post-boards gap remains.

items.question: What's the risk of preparing for both exams at once?
items.answer: Burnout, and unconsciously letting MCQ practice crowd out board-specific skills like writing derivations and long-form answers. Building in real rest and deliberately protecting board-exam-style practice time helps manage both risks.
